The First Generals Fall

Stories from the Ramayana

The First Generals Fall

Ravana's first generals fall one by one

In everyday English — Yuddha Kanda, sargas 51–59

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This book is a war story — generals come one by one, and fall. Where a general arrives, quicken your voice; where a killing comes, grow slow and grave — never shout.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Ravana furious, Hanuman thundering, Vibhishana calm.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, sargas 51–59 — the fall of Ravana's first four generals, and then Ravana himself coming to the field. The parts that speak of killing carry the ◆ mark at the top. Anything more you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — prince of Ayodhya, bearer of the bow. Warm dark-brown skin, a calm and kind face, fully clothed, barefoot in the forest.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother, slightly lighter in complexion, bow in hand.

Ravana — king of Lanka. Tall, dark-complexioned, black moustache, tall golden crown, a single head, royal robes. At the end of this book he comes to the war himself.

Sugriva — king of the vanaras, friend of Rama.

Hanuman — son of the Wind, minister of Sugriva, messenger of Rama. Light golden-brown fur, long tail, gentle devoted face, saffron dhoti. Commander at the western gate.

Angada — son of Vali, a young vanara warrior, nephew of Sugriva.

Nila — commander of the vanara army, son of Fire, master of lifting trees and boulders.

Vibhishana — Ravana's younger brother, who came to Rama's side for the sake of dharma. Calm and wise.

Dhumraksha — Ravana's first general, who comes with a great army to the western gate.

Vajradamshtra — Ravana's second general, a terrifying warrior with teeth like thunderbolts.

Akampana — Ravana's third general, whose name means “he whom none can shake” — master of every weapon, lover of battle.

Prahasta — Ravana's chief minister and the greatest name in Lanka's army, whose strength even Vibhishana speaks of.

1 · The Sound of Rejoicing · · THE SOUND OF REJOICING

Rama and Lakshmana were free — and the vanara army was roaring with joy. The sound of rejoicing reached the palaces of Lanka.

Ravana heard that sound — and started. He sent rakshasas — “Go — climb the rampart and see — what is this rejoicing?”

The rakshasas climbed the rampart — and saw — Rama and Lakshmana standing! The serpent-bonds were broken! The two brothers stood like two elephants who have snapped their fetters.

The rakshasas ran back to Ravana — “Great king! Rama and Lakshmana are alive! They stand on the battlefield — free of their bonds!”

Ravana hissed like a snake with rage. He called Dhumraksha — “Go — take a great army — and kill Rama, Lakshmana and the vanaras!”

Dhumraksha marched out of Lanka's western gate with his army — where Hanuman stood with his troops. On the way he saw ill omens — but he did not stop.

Pause and think — Ravana had announced his victory — and now he learned the announcement was false. Is hearing that a false victory was announced sadder than defeat itself? And Dhumraksha saw ill omens yet did not stop — does an order matter more than everything?

2 · Dhumraksha · · DHUMRAKSHA

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of battle and killing. Elders, please read it gently.

Dhumraksha came with his army — chariots, elephants, horses, spears and swords. A fierce battle began with the vanaras. Warriors fell on both sides.

Hanuman saw Dhumraksha killing the vanaras. He stepped forward — trees and boulders in hand. Dhumraksha shot arrows at him — but Hanuman did not stop.

Then what happened was war. Hanuman fought Dhumraksha fiercely — and at last Dhumraksha fell. His army fled — toward Lanka.

The vanaras roared. The first general had fallen — but Ravana had more names still.

Pause and think — Dhumraksha was the first general — and he fell. Does the fall of the first frighten all the rest — or anger them more? And why did Hanuman stand at the western gate — is guarding a gate also a duty?

3 · Vajradamshtra · · VAJRADAMSHTRA

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of battle and killing. Elders, please read it gently.

The news reached Ravana — Dhumraksha was dead. He grew more furious. He called Vajradamshtra — a terrifying warrior with teeth like thunderbolts, master of many divine powers.

Ravana said — “Go, Vajradamshtra! Kill Rama, Sugriva and the whole vanara army!”

Vajradamshtra came to the battlefield — and fear spread among the vanaras. His arrows covered the sky. The vanaras began to flee.

Then Angada stepped forward — son of Vali, a young vanara warrior. He fought Vajradamshtra fiercely. Vajradamshtra rained arrows on him — but Angada did not stop.

Angada struck Vajradamshtra — and he fell. The vanara army gathered around Angada and honoured him — as the gods gather around Indra.

Pause and think — Vajradamshtra's name means — teeth like thunderbolts. Does a name make a warrior — or the deed? And Angada — who is young — how did he defeat a great general — is courage greater than age?

4 · Akampana · · AKAMPANA

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of battle and killing. Elders, please read it gently.

Vajradamshtra too had fallen — so Ravana sent Akampana. Akampana — whose very name means “he whom none can shake” — master of all weapons, lover of battle.

Akampana marched to the field — but on the way he saw ill omens. He did not stop — he went on eagerly.

The battle began — and dust and wind rose. Darkness fell — neither side could see anything. Often the vanaras struck their own companions, and the rakshasas their own people.

Akampana raised his bow — and rained arrows on the vanaras. Kumuda, Mainda and Nala fought him — but he did not stop.

Then Hanuman came. He tore up a great tree — and struck it on Akampana's head. Akampana fell — and the rakshasa army fled toward Lanka.

Pause and think — Akampana's name means “he who does not tremble” — yet he fell. Can a name sometimes lie? And in dust and storm, when nothing can be seen — does fighting grow harder — or more dangerous?

5 · Prahasta Comes · · PRAHASTA COMES

Three generals had fallen — Dhumraksha, Vajradamshtra, Akampana. Ravana now called his chief minister — Prahasta. Prahasta — the greatest name in Lanka's army, without whom the army was incomplete.

Ravana said — “Prahasta, now you go. You alone are the pride of my army.”

Vibhishana told Rama — “Do not take Prahasta lightly. He is Ravana's most trusted warrior — his strength is very great.”

Prahasta came to the battlefield with his army — and began to rain arrows on the vanaras. His arrows were like serpents — and the vanaras began to fall.

Nila — commander of the vanara army — saw how much harm Prahasta was doing. He thought — “Now I myself must step forward.”

Pause and think — Ravana sent his most trusted warrior last of all. Is it right to send the greatest name last — or should he have been sent first? And Vibhishana — who knows the enemy's strength — why is his warning so important?

6 · Nila Answers · · NILA ANSWERS

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of battle and killing. Elders, please read it gently.

Nila — commander of the vanara army — fell upon Prahasta's army like a whirlwind. He was like a storm that scatters even dense clouds.

Prahasta shot serpent-like arrows at him — and Nila was wounded. But he did not stop. He tore up a great tree — and struck at Prahasta.

A fierce battle followed — vanaras and rakshasas, trees and arrows, roaring and cries. At last Nila struck Prahasta down — and Lanka's chief minister fell.

The rakshasa army fled. The vanaras roared — four generals had fallen.

Pause and think — Nila is a commander — and a commander's work is not only to give orders — it is also to step forward and fight. Is a leader the one who stands foremost? And the fall of Prahasta — was that the beginning of Ravana's defeat?

7 · Ravana Himself · · RAVANA HIMSELF

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of battle and killing. Elders, please read it gently.

Four generals had fallen — so Ravana said — “Now I will go myself.” He rode into the battlefield on his chariot — his crown gleaming, his bow drawn. His very coming was terrifying.

Ravana shot arrows at Sugriva — and Sugriva fell. Then Hanuman stepped forward — and grappled with Ravana. They struck each other with open palms — as mountain strikes mountain!

Ravana wounded Nila too with his arrows — and Nila hurled trees and a mountain at him. Ravana smashed them to pieces.

Then Ravana hurled his spear at Lakshmana — and Lakshmana fell! Rama came running — and fought Ravana fiercely. Rama broke Ravana's crown — and Ravana drew back.

(Read this part slowly — as if someone lies wounded.)

Pause and think — Ravana came himself — and Lakshmana fell. Is a king's coming himself his strength — or the sign that his army has failed? And Rama did not kill Ravana — he only broke his crown. Was that mercy — or a warning?

8 · The Field at Dusk · · THE FIELD AT DUSK

Evening was falling. The battlefield was growing quiet — the dust settling, the arrows stilling. Lakshmana was coming back to his senses — he sat up.

Rama sat beside him. Sugriva had risen too. Nila stood again. The vanara army still stood — tired, but unmoved.

Rama said — “Ravana's four generals have fallen — and he himself has drawn back. The war is not yet over — but today is ours.”

Ravana had returned to his palace — and was thinking. His army was losing. Now he would have to wake his brother — Kumbhakarna — who had been sleeping for six months.

But that story — is the next book's.

Pause and think — Four generals fell — and Ravana himself was beaten back. Can so much defeat in one day change anyone? And Rama — sitting beside Lakshmana — is his worry itself his strength?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main source

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, sargas 51–59 — the fall of Ravana's first generals.

The sound of rejoicing — sarga 51

Ravana hearing the vanaras' rejoicing; the rakshasas climbing the rampart and seeing that Rama and Lakshmana are free of their bonds; Ravana sending Dhumraksha with an army to the western gate — this is in sarga 51.

Dhumraksha — sarga 52

Dhumraksha's battle and his death at Hanuman's hands — this is in sarga 52.

Vajradamshtra — sargas 53–54

Ravana sending Vajradamshtra; Vajradamshtra spreading fear among the vanaras; Angada fighting him and killing him — this is in sargas 53–54.

Akampana — sargas 55–56

Ravana sending Akampana despite the ill omens; the battle in dust and wind; Hanuman killing Akampana with a great tree — this is in sargas 55–56.

Prahasta — sargas 57–58

Ravana sending his chief minister Prahasta; Vibhishana telling Rama of Prahasta's strength; Nila fighting Prahasta and killing him — this is in sargas 57–58.

Ravana himself — sarga 59

Ravana himself entering the battlefield; shooting arrows at Sugriva; the palm-blow duel with Hanuman; wounding Nila; hurling his spear at Lakshmana; Rama fighting Ravana, breaking his crown, and Ravana drawing back — this is in sarga 59.

About the pictures

This book's pictures show the fighting — but never death, a body, or blood. The pictures show the moment before the fight — the generals arriving, the vanaras standing against them. The killing is told only in words.

What happens next

Ravana is now thinking of waking his brother Kumbhakarna — who has been sleeping for six months. Kumbhakarna's story is the next book of this series.
